claims.text: The first prices of ShippingVnd (line 18) are returned inside four nested `if` statements (lines 11, 13, 15, 18).
The comment on line 17 reads 'charge 30000 unless the total reaches 2000000', while line 18 returns 60000 when `express` is true; the comment does not mention express.
Lines 18-19 and 22-23 of Smells.cs at stage-0 hold the same two statements, identical apart from indentation.
Because the check on line 15 only chooses between two identical pairs of lines, `weightGram` never changes the value ShippingVnd returns, for any input.

claims.text: `grep -c PATTERN FILE` writes only the number of lines of FILE that match PATTERN, and writes 0 when no line matches.
claims.source_hint: POSIX.1 utility 'grep', option -c and STDOUT section; same claim verified in foundation.l1.pipes-and-filters

claims.text: Moving the pick-up case to the top as a guard clause that returns 0 keeps every result of ShippingVnd: pick-up orders returned 0 (line 29) and still do, and every other input runs the same lines as before.

Deleting lines 15-20 of ShippingVnd (weight check, comment, first copy) keeps every result: inputs with weightGram < 5000 now run lines 22-23, which are identical to the deleted 18-19. Afterwards `weightGram` is no longer read.
Replacing a literal with a C# named constant (`const`) of the same value does not change any result: the constant's value is fixed at compile time and used where the literal was.
The C# compiler builds no code from a `//` comment such as line 17 and never compares its text with the code, so nothing checks that it still matches the line below.
If the 2000000 limit on line 18 were changed and the one on line 22 were not, orders to Hà Nội or Hồ Chí Minh under 5000 grams and from 5000 grams up would be charged against different limits.

In Samples/Oop/ShippingFee.cs, ShippingFee is the abstract base taking only the total; the sibling classes beside it give StandardShipping 30,000 below 2,000,000 and 0 from it, ExpressShipping 60,000, PickUpInStore 0. ShippingFeeTests holds two tests of them.
Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour, in small steps that each keep every result the same.
claims.source_hint: content/glossary.yaml term refactoring (short_en); standard definition of the term

claims.text: A code smell is a surface sign that points at a deeper design problem without saying what the problem is; the five named here are duplicated code, long parameter lists, comments that repeat the code, magic numbers and deep nesting.
claims.source_hint: content/glossary.yaml term code-smell; track.yaml outline item 1 of this lesson

claims.text: When a step changes any result, undo it rather than adding edits on top to fix the result, because the step was not a refactoring and a fix on top mixes two changes; then pick a smaller step.

When there are no tests, check each step by hand-tracing inputs that together reach every `return` and both sides of every `? :`, with totals just below and at the limit, and keep steps small enough to hold in your head.
Tidying first pays off when you are about to read and edit the code anyway; the behaviour change you came for is then made as a separate step with its own check.
A rewrite that changes many lines at once gives the check one answer for all edits together, so a wrong result cannot be traced to one edit by the check, unlike a chain of small checked steps.

A smell found by reading is not, by itself, evidence that a result is wrong: ShippingVnd's smells (unread `loyal`, weight check with identical branches) may hide an unwritten or wrong rule, which reading alone cannot settle.

No identifier in ShippingVnd names 2000000; only the line 17 comment hints at it. Standard shipping is free from 2000000 only for Hà Nội and Hồ Chí Minh (lines 19, 23); other cities pay 45000 standard or 90000 express at any total (line 26).
foundation.l1.small-functions presents guard clauses (returning early) as the way to keep the rest of a function flat instead of nested inside a check's `if`.
A test reports a moved result only on the inputs it actually runs, so a method having tests does not mean every changed result is caught.
claims.source_hint: follows from the gloss of 'test' in section 3 (claim 25): a test compares results for the fixed inputs it calls with, and reports nothing about other inputs

claims.text: A test, as the lesson glosses it, is code in the project that calls the method with fixed inputs and reports any result that differs; the tests at stage-0 are [Fact] methods in samples/DonHang.Samples.Tests/SamplesTests.cs.
